questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the standard way organizations validate a scoped application against an upcoming ServiceNow release is a dedicated pre-upgrade ________ instance, upgraded to the new release ahead of Production.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 describes a pre-upgrade sandbox as a sub-production instance ServiceNow upgrades to the new release ahead of production, specifically so custom applications, integrations, and customizations can be tested before anyone touches the live environment.

questions.prompt: A team already runs Dev, Test, and Production instances for a scoped application. Developers keep stepping on each other's work in Dev because half-finished changes from different people get mixed together before Test/QA ever sees them. Per Lesson 2's instance-strategy guidance, what should the team add, and why?
options: A dedicated Build instance between Dev and Test, so multiple developers' changes are merged and run together before formal Test/QA validation begins
A second Production instance, so each developer gets their own copy of live data
Nothing -- Update Set batching alone (Chapter 2) fully solves integration conflicts between developers
A fourth tier added only after the next clone refresh, since Build instances can't be added mid-quarter
questions.explain: Lesson 2 describes a Build instance as the environment where multiple developers' changes are merged and run together, catching integration problems before Test/QA testers ever see the work -- isolating 'does this work at all, together' from 'does this work correctly for a real tester.'

questions.prompt: Six months after a scoped application shipped, a team needs to roll back to how it behaved before a specific round of changes. Per Lesson 3, why is 'which Application Repository version was it' an easier question to answer at that point than 'which Update Sets, in which order'?
options: Because the Application Repository captures the whole application as one complete, numbered snapshot at publish time, while reconstructing a prior state from Update Sets means figuring out which sets, applied in what order, collectively produced it
Because Update Sets are automatically deleted from the instance after 90 days, while Application Repository versions never expire
Because Update Sets only capture UI changes, while the Application Repository also captures server-side scripts
Because the Application Repository and Update Sets track completely unrelated parts of the same application, so there's no overlap to reconstruct
questions.explain: Lesson 3 is explicit that reasoning about 'the old version of the application' purely in terms of Update Sets gets hard fast, with no single stored answer -- the Application Repository sidesteps that by treating the whole application as the versioned unit.

questions.prompt: Put these steps from the ALM Lab's scenario in the order the team actually carried them out for the quarterly refresh and the new feature release.
items: Clone Production's current Equipment Checkout data into the Dev and Test instances on the scheduled quarterly date
Run anonymization against the refreshed Dev and Test instances before any developer or tester opens them
Build and validate the new "Overdue Checkouts" escalation feature in Dev and Build
Publish a new Application Repository version capturing the entire application, including the new feature, right before it ships to Production
questions.explain: Lesson 4 walks the refresh first (clone, then anonymize before anyone opens the instance), with the feature build happening alongside, and the Application Repository version published right before the feature ships -- refresh-then-anonymize and version-before-release, in that order.

questions.prompt: In ServiceNow, what is an Update Set collision?
options: The target instance's current version of a record differs from the version captured in the Update Set being promoted
Two Update Sets on the same instance have the exact same name
An Update Set fails to open because another admin has it checked out
A Business Rule inside the Update Set throws a runtime error when the Update Set is previewed
The Update Set exceeds the maximum number of records ServiceNow allows in a single set
A scoped application's version number conflicts with an Application Repository version
questions.explain: Lesson 6 defines a collision as exactly this: the version of a record on the target instance differs from the version captured in the Update Set being promoted, presenting two competing versions -- remote and local -- for review.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes a scripting error inside a captured customization, not a collision -- a collision is specifically a mismatch between the record version in the Update Set and the record version already sitting on the target instance, which can happen even when every script inside the set is completely error-free.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the real costs of sizing Update Sets wrong, per Lesson 5.
options: Splitting every small change into its own tiny Update Set creates implicit dependencies between sets that ServiceNow doesn't track or enforce automatically
Welding several unrelated features into one broad Update Set means a bug in one feature forces you to roll back all of them together, or leave the bug live
The correct convention is to batch Update Sets by calendar day, since that's the easiest grouping for an admin to remember
A feature-sized Update Set should contain everything needed for one coherent piece of functionality, and nothing else
Update Set size has no effect on how difficult a rollback is
questions.explain: Lesson 5 rejects day-based or person-based batching in favor of feature-sized Update Sets -- too granular creates untracked dependency puzzles, too broad welds unrelated features together so a single bug forces an all-or-nothing rollback.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Chapter 2's Update-Set-at-scale lessons to what it actually means.
right: Manually combining the remote and local changes into one corrected version of a record instead of picking only one side
A commit interrupted partway through, leaving the target instance with some of the Update Set's changes applied and others not
A referenced customization that doesn't exist yet on the target instance because it lives in a different, not-yet-promoted Update Set
A change preview flags to omit rather than apply, which still needs deliberate review before being accepted
questions.explain: Missing dependency and skipped record are preview-time findings (Lesson 7); partial commit is a commit-time failure mode (also Lesson 7); reconciliation is the manual fix for a collision that touches two genuinely different parts of the same record (Lesson 6).

questions.prompt: In the Update Set Lab at Scale, put these events in the order they actually happened while the team promoted six Update Sets from Dev to Test.
items: Previewing Update Set #3 throws a missing-dependency error because it calls a Script Include that actually lives in Update Set #1
The team promotes Update Set #1 first, which previews and commits cleanly on its own
Update Set #3 is re-previewed, now resolves cleanly, and commits
Update Set #4 is found to collide with a direct change made on the Test instance, and the team reconciles both versions manually
Update Set #5 previews with two skipped records, which the team reviews individually before proceeding
Update Sets #2 and #6, which had no issues, are committed last
questions.explain: Lesson 8 walks the dependency problem on #3 to resolution first (promote #1, then re-preview #3), then the collision on #4, then the skipped records on #5, with the clean sets #2 and #6 committed only after every flagged issue was actually resolved.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 6, the dangerous default when reviewing an Update Set collision is blindly accepting the ________ version without comparing it to what's already on the target instance.
questions.explain: Lesson 6 warns that clicking 'accept remote' on every collision assumes the Update Set must be right simply because it came from the pipeline, silently throwing away a legitimate local change made directly on the target instance.

questions.prompt: A team has used Update Sets exclusively for two years on a scoped application. A new developer asks why they'd bother connecting it to a Git repository when Update Sets already move changes between instances. Per Lesson 9, what's the real answer?
options: Update Sets capture what changed between opening and closing a set, but can't show per-line diffs, full file history, isolated branches, or a pull-request review gate -- real version-control capabilities Git adds on top
Git repositories are required before an application can be scoped in Studio at all
Update Sets stop working entirely once an application has more than one developer
Connecting to Git automatically disables the need for a Dev/Test/Prod instance strategy
questions.explain: Lesson 9 is explicit that an Update Set is a point-in-time snapshot, not a replacement for real version control -- Git-based source control adds meaningful diffs, per-file blame and history, branching, and pull-request-style review that an Update Set structurally cannot provide.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before any code can move between a ServiceNow instance and its connected Git repository in either direction, the connection requires real ________ proving the instance is allowed to read from and write to that repository.
questions.explain: Lesson 10 describes configuring the credentials ServiceNow needs to authenticate as a user or service account with push and pull access, treating that credential with the same care as any other production credential.

questions.prompt: Match each source-control term from the Workflow Lab to its role in the connect-commit-review-merge cycle.
right: The application's primary, shared line of code that Test and Production are meant to reflect
An isolated line of development for one specific change, kept separate from the rest of the team's work until ready
Combining an approved feature branch's changes into the shared line of code
A proposed merge of a feature branch, opened for a teammate to read the diff, comment, and approve before it reaches the shared codebase
questions.explain: Lesson 11 walks a developer building a due-date reminder on an isolated feature branch, opening a pull request for teammate review, and merging into the main branch once approved -- the shared line Test and Production reflect.

questions.prompt: In ServiceNow's Automated Test Framework (ATF), what does the Impersonate User test step do?
options: Runs the rest of the Test as a specific user and role, so the Test actually exercises that role's UI Policies, field-level ACLs, and visibility rules
Permanently changes the record ownership of every record the Test touches to that user
Logs the named user out of all other active sessions for the duration of the Test
Grants the named user temporary admin rights so the Test can run faster
Sends a notification to the named user announcing that a test is about to run against their account
questions.explain: Lesson 13 describes Impersonate User as making the Test run as a specific, real user holding a specific role, so UI Policies and field-level ACLs conditioned on that role are actually exercised -- something an admin-only Test would never trigger.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D describes elevating a user's privileges, which is the opposite of what Impersonate User does -- it runs the Test as that specific user's actual role, restrictions and all, which is exactly what lets the Test catch a role-conditioned UI Policy or ACL bug that an admin account would never trigger.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the difference between a UI Test and a server-side Test, per Lesson 14.
options: A server-side Test can validate a Script Include's return value directly, with no form involved at all
A UI Test confirms the end-user experience works; a server-side Test confirms the underlying logic works, independent of any form
It's possible for a Script Include's logic to be completely correct while a UI Policy on the form that calls it is broken, so a server-side Test would pass while a UI Test on the same feature fails
A server-side Test and a UI Test always catch exactly the same bugs, just through a different interface
Server-side Tests are slower than UI Tests because they have to account for page-load timing
questions.explain: Lesson 14 is explicit that the two layers catch genuinely different bugs -- a server-side Test is faster precisely because it skips the UI entirely, the opposite of option E, and the two are not interchangeable, the opposite of option D.

questions.prompt: Put these Test Steps in the order a typical ATF UI Test strings them together, per Lesson 13.
items: Open a form
Set a field's value
Submit the form
Verify the result
questions.explain: Lesson 13 walks the sequence as navigating to a form, filling in a field, submitting it, and then verifying a specific concrete outcome -- the verification step is what separates a real Test from simply clicking through blindly.

questions.prompt: Match each ATF concept to what it actually is.
right: Automated running of a Test Suite on a defined, recurring schedule
A single, reusable action -- opening a form, setting a field, checking a result
A sequence of Test Steps run in order that together simulate one real scenario start to finish
A grouping of multiple individual Tests that run together as one coordinated set with a combined pass/fail result
questions.explain: Lessons 12 and 15 build this hierarchy directly: Test Steps compose a Test, Tests group into a Test Suite, and a Test Suite can run automatically via Scheduled Test Execution.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: configuring a Test Suite to run automatically on a defined, recurring schedule -- rather than only when someone remembers to click Run Test -- is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 names this mechanism Scheduled Test Execution, the same underlying idea as Scheduled Jobs, closing the gap where nobody tests on the days nobody happens to think of it.

questions.prompt: In the ATF Lab, the server-side Test for EquipmentAvailabilityChecker creates a GlideRecord representing equipment that's already checked out, then calls isEquipmentAvailable() against that same equipment's ID. What should the Test assert, and why build this as a separate server-side Test instead of relying on the UI Test alone?
options: Assert the method returns false, because the equipment is checked out -- and build it separately because a server-side Test validates the exact logic the before-insert Business Rule depends on, independent of any form, UI Policy, or role
Assert the method returns true, because the UI Test already confirmed the employee's request was approved
Assert the method throws an error, because querying checked-out equipment is an invalid operation
There's no need for a separate server-side Test -- the UI Test's 'Verify the result' step already proves the Script Include's logic is correct
questions.explain: Lesson 16's lab asserts isEquipmentAvailable() returns false for already-checked-out equipment, and builds this as a server-side Test specifically because it validates the Script Include directly, independent of any form, UI Policy, or role.

questions.prompt: A team's GitHub Actions pipeline can already build, test, and deploy a scoped application entirely on its own, with no ServiceNow instance involved in triggering any of it. Per Lesson 17, why does this team still need something like the ServiceNow DevOps app?
options: Left alone, the pipeline has no reason to know ServiceNow's Change Management process exists, so code can reach production entirely outside governed Change Enablement -- the DevOps app is what connects pipeline events to real, governed Change Request records
Because GitHub Actions cannot deploy ServiceNow scoped applications without the DevOps app installed as a plugin inside the pipeline itself
Because ATF tests can only run if the ServiceNow DevOps app is present on the instance
Because Update Sets stop functioning once a pipeline tool is introduced
questions.explain: Lesson 17 frames ServiceNow DevOps as the bridge between 'code is moving through a pipeline somewhere else' and 'ServiceNow knows about it and is tracking it the governed way,' closing a governance gap pure CI/CD tooling leaves wide open.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how mature ServiceNow DevOps implementations resolve the change-velocity-vs-change-control tension, per Lesson 19.
options: A change with strong, passing ATF coverage has real automated evidence of low risk, which can justify routing it through a pre-approved Standard Change template
A change that's genuinely high-business-risk, such as one touching approval authority, can still warrant full CAB review even if every automated test passes
Passing ATF tests and low business risk are the same measurement, so a green test suite is always sufficient justification for fast-tracking
Blanket fast-tracking every pipeline deployment throws away exactly what Change Enablement exists to catch
Blanket gatekeeping of every pipeline-driven change through full CAB review has no real downside
questions.explain: Lesson 19 is explicit that test coverage and business risk are related but not the same measurement, and that mature implementations differentiate by risk rather than picking blanket fast-tracking or blanket gatekeeping, both of which have real downsides.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a change backed by strong ATF coverage can be routed through a pre-approved, fast, low-friction category of Change Request called a ________ Change template.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 ties strong ATF coverage to Course 8's Standard Change template, a pre-approved category for well-understood, low-risk, repeatable work.

questions.prompt: Put these pipeline stages in the order they occur in Lesson 18's build-test-deploy flow, as each one gets reported back to ServiceNow DevOps.
items: Build stage -- a developer's commit triggers the pipeline to build the application
Test stage -- automated tests, potentially including ATF tests, run against the build
Deploy stage -- the pipeline deploys the change, and ServiceNow DevOps creates or updates the corresponding Change Request
questions.explain: Lesson 18 walks the flow in exactly this order, noting the deploy stage is the event that matters most to Change Management since it's what triggers the Change Request.

questions.prompt: Two pull requests merge against the Equipment Checkout application in the same week. Change A fixes a confusing field label and a validation message, with a new passing UI test covering exactly that message. Change B updates the server-side logic that decides which manager must approve a high-value checkout request, with the full ATF suite passing including server-side tests on the approval logic. Per Lesson 20, why do these get routed differently?
options: Change A's passing test evidence is direct evidence about a narrow, low-business-risk change, which fits a Standard Change template -- Change B's passing tests only prove the code does what existing tests check for, not that the new approval-routing rule is correct for every real scenario, so its high business risk still warrants full CAB review
Change B gets the Standard Change template because server-side tests are considered more rigorous than UI tests
Both changes should get the exact same routing, since both had a clean pipeline build and a fully passing ATF suite
Change A requires CAB review because label and validation-message changes are historically the riskiest category of change
questions.explain: Lesson 20's own reasoning is that the deciding factor was never whether the pipeline succeeded -- it was what the change actually touched, and whether the passing test coverage was evidence about the part of the system carrying the real business risk.

questions.prompt: A scoped application deploys to Production with zero technical defects -- every dependency was already present, and the Update Sets were sequenced correctly. Users still flood the help desk with complaints the moment it goes live, because nobody told them the feature they use daily would look different afterward. Per Lesson 21, which of the three deployment-planning questions did this deployment skip?
options: Communication -- proactively notifying affected users beforehand is part of what makes a deployment actually succeed from the business's point of view, not a courtesy layered on top
Sequencing -- the dependency order must have been wrong even though no preview errors appeared
Timing -- the deployment must have happened during a scheduled Change freeze
None of the three -- a deployment with zero technical defects and correct sequencing has, by definition, nothing left to go wrong
questions.explain: Lesson 21 is explicit that sequencing can be perfect and timing can be a legitimate low-traffic window, and a deployment can still cause a support ticket storm purely because nobody told affected users what was changing.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the real decision criteria for choosing revert vs. roll forward, per Lesson 22.
options: Severity and scope -- how serious the issue is and how many users or workflows it affects -- pulls the decision toward whichever path gets back to a working state fastest
Roll forward is the right call when the root cause is already understood and the fix is small and low-risk
A messy, overly broad deployment with scattered, partially-applied changes can actually be harder to cleanly revert than to simply fix forward
A revert should always be preferred over a roll-forward fix, regardless of what broke
Reverting is only possible if the team is using Update Sets, not Source Control or the Application Repository
questions.explain: Lesson 22 names three real decision drivers -- severity/scope, confidence in a roll-forward fix, and how clean a revert would actually be -- and is explicit that neither revert nor roll forward is automatically the right answer.

questions.prompt: Match each rollback-related term to its definition.
right: Leaving a deployment in place and shipping a small, targeted corrective fix instead of undoing it
A revert that undoes only the broken change, without undoing other working functionality bundled in the same deployment
Restoring the exact prior state using a previous Application Repository version, Update Set, or Source Control commit
How serious an issue is and how many users or workflows it actually affects
questions.explain: Lesson 22 defines revert as restoring the exact prior state, roll forward as a targeted fix on top of the live deployment, severity/scope as the first real decision criterion, and a clean revert as one that undoes only the broken piece.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the tool that gives a visual view of everything already scheduled against the target instance for a given deployment window is the ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 21 names the Change Calendar as the tool for checking what's already scheduled on the target instance, used alongside Conflict Detection before committing to a deployment time.

questions.prompt: The Course Registration capstone treats the three-instance Dev/Test/Prod pipeline as non-negotiable, including a flat rule that no 'quick fix' ever touches Prod directly. Per Lesson 24, what's the real reason a direct quick fix in Prod is rejected, even for something small?
options: A quick fix made directly in Prod has no corresponding record anywhere else and creates drift the moment anyone tries to promote the next real change through Dev and Test
ServiceNow technically blocks any direct configuration change made on a Production instance
Quick fixes are allowed in Prod as long as they're documented afterward in a comment on the Change Request
The three-instance pipeline exists only to satisfy the registrar's IT director's request for 'a paper trail,' with no functional purpose beyond that
questions.explain: Lesson 24 states this plainly: a quick fix made directly in Prod has no corresponding record anywhere else and creates drift the moment anyone tries to promote the next real change -- which is why the three-instance pipeline is treated as non-negotiable.

questions.prompt: Put these items from the capstone's pre-deployment checklist and rollback plan in the order Lesson 26 presents them as required steps before, and immediately after, a production promotion.
items: Confirm the "Course Registration -- Critical Path" ATF Test Suite passed against the candidate change in Test, with no failing or skipped tests
Confirm dependent changes, such as a new field and the Flow Action that reads it, are sequenced to commit in the correct order
Confirm the Change Request has the ATF Suite's pass result attached as evidence and has been formally approved by the CAB
If the ATF Suite re-run against Prod fails within the first hour, begin rollback immediately and notify the registrar's office and IT director as it starts
questions.explain: Lesson 26 lists the pre-deployment checklist in this order -- tests passing, dependencies sequenced, Change Request approved -- before describing the rollback trigger and immediate communication that follow a failed post-deployment re-check.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the ATF coverage the capstone designs for Course Registration's critical path, per Lesson 25.
options: The full-section rejection path gets its own explicit UI Test rather than being assumed to work 'by extension' once the happy-path test passes

The server-side capacity-check Test is necessary even though the UI Test already exercises that logic indirectly, because it catches a bug in the capacity math itself independent of any future UI change
A rejected registration attempt must not decrement the section's open-seat count, and the happy-path test confirms the open-seat count DOES decrement by exactly one on success
Only one test is needed for the critical path, since 'a student registers for a course' is a single scenario
The three tests are grouped into one Test Suite configured to run only right before a production release, not on every pipeline build
questions.explain: Lesson 25 builds three distinct tests -- happy-path UI, full-section-rejection UI, and server-side capacity-check -- grouped into a Test Suite that runs on every pipeline build, precisely because the critical path covers two distinct scenarios that a single test can't prove.
